name: The road from Aswan to Luxor: three Ptolemaic temples in a day
note: Orientation: 215 km, Kom Ombo (45 km), Edfu (105 km), Esna (155 km); all three are Ptolemaic/Roman (305 BC-250 AD) when Greek kings dressed as pharaohs to keep the priests on side; why they are so well preserved (sand, later dates, villages built over them); timing and heat; how to recognise a Ptolemaic temple (deep-cut relief, composite capitals, screen walls, mammisi, crypts).

name: How a Ptolemaic temple works: a walk from light to dark
note: Pylon as horizon hieroglyph, the open court for the public, the pronaos with screen walls, the hypostyle, the offering hall, the sanctuary with the naos and the barque: floor rising, ceiling lowering, light fading toward the god's dark home; the ambulatory, crypts, stairs to the roof for the New Year ritual; the mammisi; the sacred lake; the enclosure wall as the waters of chaos; who was allowed where.

name: Temple of Kom Ombo: one temple, two gods
note: Ptolemy VI to Roman; unique symmetrical double plan: south half for Sobek the crocodile god (with Hathor and Khonsu), north half for Haroeris 'Horus the Elder' (with Tasenetnofret and Panebtawy); two entrances, two sanctuaries side by side; built on a bend where crocodiles basked; much lost to the river and to the 1893 sugar factory; the view at sunset; the drowned Nubians resettled in 'New Nubia' here after 1964.

name: The surgical instruments relief
note: On the inner face of the outer corridor (back wall): a Roman-period relief of scalpels, forceps, saws, bone-saws, suction cups, scales and a birthing chair offered to the god, with two goddesses on birthing stools; probably a healing-cult list rather than a 'hospital'; link to Egyptian medicine (Edwin Smith papyrus) and to Imhotep; find it on the rear wall near the Nilometer.

name: The festival calendar relief
note: In the offering hall area: a carved list of festival days with offerings, a chance to read Egyptian numerals (strokes, hobbles, coils, lotus) and the 365-day civil calendar (12 x 30 + 5 epagomenal days), the seasons Akhet, Peret, Shemu; the Sothic rising of Sirius; good place to teach reading numbers.

name: The twin sanctuaries, the crypts and the Nilometer
note: The two granite pedestals for the sacred barques; the hidden corridor between the sanctuaries where a priest could 'speak' as the oracle; the crypts under the floor; the deep circular Nilometer well and the crocodile basin outside; the Ptolemy XII and Cleopatra VII reliefs (Cleopatra with Ptolemy XV?) on the pylon remains; the lion-headed drains.

name: The Crocodile Museum
note: Small 2012 museum by the exit: ~20 of the 300 crocodile mummies from the nearby necropolis, some 4 m, with gold-leaf eyes and baby crocodiles on their backs; crocodile eggs and foetuses; the bronze and wooden crocodile statues; how and why Sobek's animals were raised in the temple pool, fed honey cakes, adorned with earrings (Herodotus); free with the ticket, air-conditioned.

name: Sobek: the crocodile who made the Nile
note: Fertility and the river's power, the Faiyum cult (Crocodilopolis, Shedet), merged as Sobek-Ra; the ambiguity of a god who is also the beast that eats you; Amenemhat III's devotion; the Greek name Suchos; the live crocodile oracle; crocodiles returned to Lake Nasser after the dam.

name: Temple of Horus at Edfu: the best-preserved temple in Egypt
note: 237-57 BC (Ptolemy III to XII, 180 years), buried to the lintels under sand and houses until Mariette cleared it in 1860; complete roof, every room, 36 m pylon; the building texts that record how it was built and what each room was for; the horse-carriage arrival (animal welfare caveat); 2 hours; the order to walk; the 'Myth of Horus' on the enclosure wall; the falcon statue photo.

name: The pylon, the falcon statues and the court
commons: Edfu temple pylon falcon statue Horus
note: Pylon of Ptolemy XII smiting enemies before Horus and Hathor (the same king as at Philae), grooves for flagpoles, the stairs inside (not open); the court of 32 columns with varied capitals; the pair of black granite falcons wearing the double crown, one intact, the most photographed statue in Upper Egypt; the reliefs of the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting around the court.

name: Hypostyle halls, the library, the laboratory and the sanctuary
commons: Edfu temple sanctuary naos Nectanebo barque
note: First hypostyle with 12 columns and the two small rooms: the 'House of Books' library with its catalogue of papyri carved on the wall, and the 'House of the Morning' robing room; the second hypostyle and the 'laboratory' with perfume and incense recipes carved in the walls (kyphi); the offering hall; the sanctuary with the polished granite naos of Nectanebo II (the oldest thing here, 360 BC) and a modern replica of the barque; the ceiling soot from Christian squatters; the Nilometer and the stairs to the roof with the New Year procession reliefs.

name: The Triumph of Horus: the sacred drama on the west wall
wiki: The Contendings of Horus and Seth
commons: Edfu Horus harpooning Seth hippopotamus relief
note: Inner face of the enclosure wall (west side of the ambulatory): the annual mystery play in which Horus harpoons Seth as a tiny hippopotamus ten times (ritually small so the evil is weak), the king and Isis watching, the hippo cake cut and eaten at the end; the 'Legend of the Winged Disc' where Horus of Behdet flies as the sun to defeat the enemies: origin of the winged sun over every door; the text is one of the few Egyptian dramas with stage directions.

name: The mammisi and the Feast of the Beautiful Meeting
commons: Edfu mammisi birth house Bes columns
note: The birth house outside the pylon, with Bes on the column abaci and the birth of Harsomtus; each year in the third month of summer Hathor sailed 160 km upriver from Dendera to spend two weeks with Horus here: the Beautiful Meeting, a honeymoon festival with the whole town drunk; the Festival of Victory re-enacting the Seth drama; the Coronation of the Sacred Falcon when a live falcon was crowned.

name: Horus: the falcon, the king and the eye
note: Sky god whose eyes are sun and moon; the many Horuses (Horus the Elder/Haroeris at Kom Ombo, Horus of Behdet at Edfu, Horus the Child/Harpocrates at Philae, Horus son of Isis); every living king as Horus; the Eye lost to Seth and healed by Thoth as the symbol of wholeness (the wedjat you see everywhere, the pharmacy symbol legend); link to the Osiris myth.

name: Temple of Khnum at Esna: the hall under the town
note: Only the Roman hypostyle hall (Claudius to Decius, 1st-3rd c. AD) survives, 9 m below the modern street in a pit because the town grew over it; the rest of the Ptolemaic temple lies under the houses; 24 columns with 18 different lotus/palm capitals; Napoleon's savants, Champollion; the reopened painted ceiling (see next); the Esna barrage; short visit, 30-45 min, after the souq street walk down.

name: The restored ceiling: zodiac, vultures and 2,000 years of soot removed
commons: Esna temple ceiling restored colours zodiac
note: 2018-2024 Egyptian-German project (Tübingen, Christian Leitz; Ministry of Antiquities) cleaned soot, bird droppings and salt to reveal original colours: 46 vultures and winged snakes (Nekhbet and Wadjet) in the central aisle, the Egyptian and Babylonian/Greek zodiac (Sagittarius with a scorpion tail, Pisces), the decans, the sky goddess; hidden texts in colour only, never carved; it is the most complete painted temple ceiling in Egypt now.

name: Khnum's crossword hymns: a text written only in crocodiles
commons: Esna temple hieroglyphs crocodile hymn column
note: On two columns, hymns to Khnum written cryptographically: one almost entirely with crocodile signs, another with ram signs: priestly wordplay of the Roman period when hieroglyphs became a secret game with 1,000+ signs; the Esna festival calendar; the creation text where Khnum fashions humans on the potter's wheel, including the detailed anatomy ('he made the hair sprout, the skin cover the flesh'); the Latin-period emperors in pharaoh's dress (Trajan, Hadrian, Decius).

name: Khnum: the potter who shaped people
note: Ram-headed creator who forms each person and their ka on a potter's wheel (shown in Hatshepsut's birth reliefs, 21 Oct), guardian of the Nile's source at Elephantine, lord of Esna with his consorts Neith (here as creator too) and Menhit; the Famine Stela on Sehel island (Djoser's dream); the horizontal-horned ancient ram species.
